latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Loss of colonization resistance after antibacterial exposure, hospitalization, long-term care residence, gastric acid suppression, chemotherapy, or critical illness permits toxigenic C. difficile spores to germinate and dominate the colonic niche.

Vegetative C. difficile proliferation with toxin A, toxin B, and sometimes binary toxin production. This is the direct antimicrobial target of enteral vancomycin, fidaxomicin, metronidazole exposure in inflamed tissue, and microbiome restoration.
TcdA/TcdB glucosylate Rho-family GTPases, disrupt actin cytoskeleton, loosen tight junctions, trigger epithelial necrosis, and expose lamina propria to neutrophilic inflammation.

Dense neutrophilic exudate, fibrin, mucus, and necrotic epithelium form pseudomembranes and marked colonic wall edema. This drives leukemoid reaction, hypoalbuminemia, pain, wall thickening, and pseudomembranes on endoscopy or pathology.

Mucosal injury and inflammation cause chloride-rich watery stool loss, vomiting, poor intake, third spacing, and prerenal physiology. In fulminant disease diarrhea can decrease or disappear when ileus dominates.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Inflammatory colonic dysmotility, ileus, and toxic megacolon
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Inflammation penetrates into muscularis propria and enteric neural control, impairing smooth muscle tone and causing ileus, gas trapping, severe distension, and toxic megacolon with perforation risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Gut barrier failure and bacterial translocation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Severe mucosal necrosis and dysbiosis permit enteric bacteria, endotoxin, and inflammatory mediators to cross the gut barrier, producing secondary bacteremia, peritonitis physiology, and refractory shock.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic inflammatory shock and organ dysfunction
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Cytokine surge, volume depletion, bacterial translocation, and capillary leak produce fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, hypotension, lactic acidosis, AKI, respiratory failure, encephalopathy, and vasopressor-dependent shock.
Pressure, ischemia, transmural necrosis, or toxic megacolon rupture produces perforation, feculent peritonitis, abrupt source-control need, and a sharp mortality increase.

Ongoing toxin production, ileus-limited drug delivery, necrotic colon, toxic megacolon, or perforation risk persists despite medical therapy. This mechanism falls after effective colectomy, diverting loop ileostomy with lavage, or successful rescue microbiome therapy.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Loss of colonization resistance permits spores to germinate and vegetative organisms to dominate.
Toxigenic burden is the upstream source of toxin A/B exposure.
Epithelial necrosis and cytokine release recruit neutrophils and fibrinopurulent exudate.
Barrier and ion-transport injury cause watery diarrhea, vomiting, poor intake, and third spacing.
Transmural inflammation and edema impair motility and set up ileus and megacolon.
Distension, edema, and pressure compromise mucosal perfusion and worsen gut-barrier leak.
Severe epithelial necrosis allows enteric organisms and endotoxin to translocate even before perforation.
Endotoxin and bacterial translocation amplify shock beyond toxin colitis alone.
Hypovolemia and renal hypoperfusion lower physiologic reserve and worsen lactate.
Pressure and ischemic injury during toxic megacolon are major routes to perforation.
Uncontrolled colon focus and poor intraluminal drug delivery sustain organism and toxin burden.
Persistent uncontrolled colitis drives ongoing shock physiology and organ dysfunction.
Recent high-risk antibacterial exposure is a measurable upstream context for microbiome disruption.
Hospital and long-term care exposure increase both spore exposure and antibiotic pressure.
Toxin injury produces watery or sometimes bloody diarrhea unless ileus suppresses stool output.
Colitis and distension produce cramps, diffuse pain, and tenderness.
Severe enterocolitis, ileus, and shock commonly cause nausea and vomiting.
Severe CDI often produces marked neutrophilic leukocytosis or leukemoid reaction.
Neutrophilic predominance is a core inflammatory signature of pseudomembranous colitis.
IL-6-driven acute-phase response tracks severe colitis burden.
Protein-losing colitis, capillary leak, and inflammation lower serum albumin.
Edematous colitis produces CT wall thickening and thumbprinting.
Pseudomembranes are the visible/pathologic expression of fibrinopurulent mucosal injury.
Volume depletion and shock raise creatinine above baseline.
Volume depletion and septic hypoperfusion increase AKI event risk.
Ileus and gas trapping produce progressive abdominal distension.
Fulminant CDI may present with ileus and reduced diarrhea.
Long absence of bowel movement marks paralytic ileus and impaired intraluminal antibiotic delivery.
Toxic megacolon is defined by marked colonic dilation, often exceeding 6 cm and sometimes far higher.
Colonic dysmotility, systemic toxicity, and progressive dilation drive toxic megacolon event risk.
Ileus and vomiting reduce reliable delivery of oral or nasogastric vancomycin to the diseased bowel.
Severe CDI can permit secondary bloodstream infection with enteric organisms.
Systemic cytokine response produces fever; frail or immunosuppressed patients may be afebrile or hypothermic.
Fever, hypovolemia, pain, and shock raise heart rate.
Metabolic acidosis, abdominal pressure, and shock increase ventilatory drive.
Fulminant disease can progress to distributive or mixed shock.
MAP falls with vasoplegia, hypovolemia, and cardiopulmonary decompensation.
Lactate rises with hypoperfusion and persistent severe inflammatory shock.
Severe colitis with bacterial translocation or septic physiology can raise procalcitonin.
Shock, fever, sedatives, and critical illness can produce confusion, obtundation, or coma.
Abdominal pressure, aspiration, pneumonia, ARDS, or shock can lower oxygenation in severe cases.
Systemic inflammatory shock activity is the direct hazard state for vasopressor-dependent shock.
Respiratory failure can arise from shock, abdominal compartment pressure, aspiration, or ARDS.
Transmural necrosis and toxic megacolon are the immediate substrates for perforation.
Perforation or transmural necrosis produces peritoneal inflammation.
Perforation, toxic megacolon, necrosis, or refractory fulminant colitis requires surgical source-control consideration.
Persistent uncontrolled colitis is the inverse of adequate source control.
Shock and organ dysfunction dominate near-term mortality in fulminant CDI.
Perforation and feculent peritonitis sharply increase death hazard.
Persistent uncontrolled toxin colitis despite medical therapy increases mortality unless effective source control or rescue therapy succeeds.
AKI marks severe hypoperfusion and worsens fluid, drug, and acid-base management.
Toxic megacolon is the major pre-perforation state associated with urgent surgery and high mortality.

axes.shape_free_text: Exposure within the prior 1-12 weeks to high-risk antibiotics such as clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, broad beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors, carbapenems, or prolonged/multiple antibacterial courses.
Recent hospitalization, ICU stay, nursing home residence, long-term care, or shared healthcare environment with high spore exposure.
Fever is common in severe CDI; hypothermia or absence of fever can occur in elderly, frail, immunosuppressed, or late shock states.
Tachycardia from fever, pain, hypovolemia, shock, adrenergic stress, or respiratory failure.
Tachypnea from metabolic acidosis, abdominal pressure, fever, sepsis, aspiration, pneumonia, or ARDS.
Falls with hypovolemia and septic shock; may be confounded by comorbid adrenergic crisis or chronic hypertension.
Low MAP reflects shock physiology; resuscitation and vasopressors aim to restore perfusion.
Usually normal in isolated colitis; can fall with aspiration, pneumonia, abdominal pressure, ARDS, or shock.
Confusion, obtundation, delirium, coma, or inability to assess due to sedation in severe shock or critical illness.
Watery diarrhea is typical; may be non-bloody or bloody. In fulminant ileus, diarrhea can be minimal or absent despite severe disease.
Nausea or vomiting from severe enterocolitis, ileus, abdominal distension, or shock.
Cramping, diffuse pain, tenderness, or peritoneal pain; can be mild despite severe dilation in neurologic impairment or sedation.
Progressive bloating, tense abdomen, visible distension, or CT distension from ileus or toxic megacolon.
Paralytic ileus, obstipation, reduced bowel sounds, no bowel movement, or imaging with air-fluid levels and diffuse bowel dilation.
Duration without bowel movement when ileus/obstipation is present; child measurement should be consumed only if ileus is clinically present.
Largest colonic diameter on CT or abdominal radiograph. Values above 6 cm support toxic megacolon physiology; very high values indicate perforation risk.
CT or gross/pathology evidence of edematous thickened colon or small bowel wall from pseudomembranous inflammation.
Endoscopic, gross, or histologic pseudomembranes. In case JSON this should usually be stored under confirmatory_findings rather than ordinary observations.
Often greater than 15 in severe CDI and can exceed 30-50 in fulminant disease; leukopenia in critical illness is possible but less typical.
Neutrophilic predominance is common in severe pseudomembranous colitis.
Acute-phase inflammation marker; often elevated in severe colitis but not specific.
Can rise with septic physiology or bacterial translocation; not specific for CDI and may stay modest in isolated toxin colitis.
Elevated lactate signals shock, hypoperfusion, or impending surgical catastrophe; high or rising values strongly worsen prognosis.
Rises above baseline from dehydration, AKI, shock, CKD background, or nephrotoxic exposures.
Low albumin reflects protein-losing colitis, capillary leak, malnutrition, frailty, and severity.
May be normal; can fall with critical illness, bleeding, hemodilution, or chronic disease.
Hazard of systemic toxicity with marked colonic dilation, ileus, and perforation risk.
Hazard of colonic perforation from toxic megacolon, transmural necrosis, or severe pressure ischemia.
Rebound, guarding, acute surgical abdomen, free air/fluid with clinical peritonitis, or feculent contamination.
Hazard of progression to fluid-refractory hypotension or vasopressor-dependent shock.
AKI hazard from dehydration, septic shock, nephrotoxins, or baseline renal vulnerability.
Hazard of intubation or ongoing mechanical ventilation from respiratory failure, aspiration, ARDS, shock, or severe abdominal pressure.
Probability that secondary enteric bacteremia reflects severe mucosal barrier failure during CDI rather than an independent primary source.
Reliability of oral or nasogastric medication delivery to diseased bowel; low with vomiting, ileus, NPO status, shock, or severe distension.
Feasibility of rectal retention vancomycin reaching the colon; reduced by rectal stump anatomy, perforation, severe procedural risk, or inability to retain enemas.

Need for colectomy, diverting loop ileostomy with lavage, bowel resection, or other non-antibiotic source-control intervention when toxic megacolon, perforation, necrosis, or refractory fulminant colitis is present.
Adequacy of non-antibiotic control of necrotic, dilated, perforated, or medically refractory bowel source; rises after effective colectomy, diversion/lavage, or successful rescue strategy.
Hazard of recurrent CDI after initial clinical response; driven by persistent spores, impaired microbiome recovery, advanced age, immunosuppression, and ongoing antibiotics.
Procedure- or critical-illness-related major bleeding hazard, relevant around colectomy, lavage, coagulopathy, transfusion, or anticoagulation.

Aggregate lifespan hazard from fulminant toxin colitis, shock, ileus/toxic megacolon, AKI, respiratory failure, bacterial translocation, perforation, surgical risk, frailty, and source-control failure.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Ileus prevents enteral vancomycin from reliably reaching distal diseased bowel.
Bedside distension tracks radiographic dilation, though obesity, ascites, and sedation can weaken the link.
Marked colonic dilation is the imaging substrate of toxic megacolon.
Toxic megacolon can transition to perforation if pressure and ischemia continue.
Perforation produces peritoneal contamination and peritonitis.
Peritonitis is an acute surgical source-control state.
Adequate colectomy, diversion/lavage, or rescue strategy terminates persistent uncontrolled focus.
Worsening shock increases lactate; restoring perfusion should lower lactate.
Persistent hyperlactatemia is a strong marker of refractory shock or bowel catastrophe.
Leukemoid reaction correlates with fulminant colitis burden and worse prognosis.
Hypoalbuminemia marks severe protein-losing colitis, frailty, and capillary leak.
Creatinine rise signals AKI or renal vulnerability.
Vasopressor-dependent shock is a dominant mortality driver in fulminant CDI.
Perforation sharply increases death hazard through peritonitis and uncontrolled source.
Respiratory failure and mechanical ventilation mark critical illness severity.
Recurrent severe CDI increases later hospitalization and death risk, though less acutely than shock/perforation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Stopping avoidable non-CDI antibacterial pressure helps microbiome recovery and reduces ongoing dysbiosis.
Concurrent bacteremia or another uncontrolled infection may require continuing non-CDI antibiotics despite CDI risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Removes avoidable dysbiosis pressure; not adequate as sole therapy for severe/fulminant CDI.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe ileus or vomiting can prevent oral/NG vancomycin from reaching the distal colon.
Ileus lowers intraluminal delivery and makes rectal or surgical delivery paths more important.

treatments.context_specific_role: Main intraluminal antimicrobial pressure against toxigenic C. difficile when the bowel can receive enteral drug.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Systemic metronidazole can reach inflamed tissue when enteral delivery is unreliable.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adds systemic anaerobic activity during fulminant disease, especially with ileus; should not be the only active CDI therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Anatomy, retention failure, severe procedural risk, or perforation can prevent effective rectal delivery.
Instrumentation or enema pressure can be hazardous when perforation is imminent or present.

side_effects.interpretation: Risk is small but clinically relevant when colon is severely dilated, ischemic, or perforated.

treatments.context_specific_role: Improves local vancomycin delivery in ileus, usually alongside enteral vancomycin and IV metronidazole.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Enteral delivery still depends on drug reaching diseased bowel.
Microbiome-sparing activity matters more when recurrence risk is high.

treatments.context_specific_role: Useful enteral CDI antimicrobial with less collateral microbiome injury; acute fulminant use depends on delivery and patient context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Benefit is mainly prevention of recurrence, not immediate decompression or shock reversal.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct to lower recurrence risk after the acute episode is controlled; does not replace antimicrobial therapy or surgery.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Perforation or acute surgical abdomen changes the problem to operative source control.
Toxic megacolon with impending perforation may not have time for microbiome rescue alone.

treatments.context_specific_role: Microbiome rescue for recurrent or selected refractory severe/fulminant CDI when delivery and safety are acceptable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Colectomy is a source-control intervention, so its benefit appears when the colon itself is the uncontrolled lethal focus.
Very high lactate indicates high operative risk but also urgent uncontrolled shock.

side_effects.interpretation: Emergency colectomy during shock carries bleeding and procedural complication risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Removes the uncontrolled colon source in toxic megacolon, perforation, necrosis, or medically refractory fulminant colitis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Established perforation or necrotic colon may require colectomy rather than diversion/lavage alone.

side_effects.interpretation: Operative diversion still carries bleeding and postoperative complication risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Provides diversion, lavage, and antegrade intraluminal vancomycin delivery while attempting colon preservation in selected fulminant cases.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluid benefit is greatest when hypovolemia or septic hypoperfusion is present.

treatments.context_specific_role: Restores intravascular volume during diarrhea, vomiting, third spacing, and shock; does not reduce toxin burden.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vasopressor support matters when hypotension persists despite fluids.

treatments.context_specific_role: Perfusion support during fluid-refractory shock; source control and CDI therapy must still address the driver.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ventilation support is useful when respiratory failure or airway protection need is active.

treatments.context_specific_role: Organ support for respiratory failure or airway protection during fulminant CDI critical illness.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Benefit appears when AKI complications such as acidosis, hyperkalemia, uremia, or volume overload are present.

side_effects.interpretation: Catheter placement and anticoagulation can increase bleeding risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Support for severe AKI complications during fulminant CDI; not antimicrobial or source-control therapy.

clindamycin_fluoroquinolone_cephalospori.trajectory_modulation: Stronger microbiome disruption and higher toxigenic burden probability.

multiple_or_prolonged_antibiotics.trajectory_modulation: Greater and longer dysbiosis; slower recovery unless antibiotics can be stopped.

present.trajectory_modulation: Higher spore exposure, more antibiotic pressure, and more severe comorbidity burden.

age_65_to_80.trajectory_modulation: Higher severe CDI and recurrence risk.

age_over_80_or_frail.trajectory_modulation: Higher ileus, shock, AKI, recurrence, and mortality risk; fever and pain can be blunted.

present.trajectory_modulation: Higher severe disease, secondary infection, and poor healing risk; fever or leukocytosis may be blunted depending on immune status.
Higher baseline creatinine and less reserve during fluid loss or shock.
Greater baseline colitis activity and higher risk of diagnostic overlap, severe colitis, toxic dilation, and colectomy.

proton_pump_inhibitor_or_h2_blocker.trajectory_modulation: Raises susceptibility through altered upper GI and colonic ecology; effect size is weaker than recent antibiotics.

ribotype_027_or_binary_toxin_context.trajectory_modulation: Higher toxin production, fluoroquinolone resistance context, leukocytosis, toxic megacolon, recurrence, and outbreak potential.

unavoidable_due_to_concurrent_infection.trajectory_modulation: Sustains dysbiosis and recurrence hazard; may weaken deescalation benefit.

heart_failure_low_ejection_fraction_or_m.trajectory_modulation: Does not specifically cause CDI but magnifies shock, respiratory failure, surgical mortality, and fluid/vasopressor tradeoffs.

present.trajectory_modulation: Higher recurrence hazard and spore persistence; microbiome restoration and recurrence modifiers become more important.

supportive_care: Immediate contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene and sporicidal environmental cleaning.
Stop avoidable inciting antibiotics, antimotility agents, and unnecessary gastric acid suppression when clinically feasible.
Early ICU-level monitoring for hypotension, ileus, toxic megacolon, rising lactate, AKI, altered mental status, or respiratory failure.
Frequent abdominal exams and low threshold for serial abdominal radiograph or CT when distension, ileus, pain, fever, leukocytosis, or shock worsens.
Early surgical consultation for fulminant disease, toxic megacolon, perforation concern, peritonitis, worsening organ failure, or nonresponse to maximal medical therapy.
Bowel rest and nasogastric decompression when ileus, severe vomiting, or marked distension is present.
Aggressive but reassessed IV fluid resuscitation; avoid fluid overload in heart failure, renal failure, or severe abdominal pressure states.
Vasopressor support for fluid-refractory shock while source and toxin burden are addressed.
Track WBC, creatinine, lactate, albumin, electrolytes, hemoglobin, CRP or other inflammatory markers, urine output, and acid-base status serially.
Correct electrolyte derangements and dehydration; avoid hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia that may worsen ileus.
Mechanical ventilation and aspiration prevention when respiratory failure, abdominal pressure, or impaired mental status threatens oxygenation or airway protection.
Renal replacement support when AKI complications require it.
Nutritional support after ileus improves; avoid premature enteral loading during severe toxic megacolon or bowel obstruction physiology.
Assess recurrence risk after response and plan follow-up, antimicrobial stewardship, and recurrence prevention strategy.
Do not use toxin/PCR positivity alone as ordinary ranking evidence; interpret confirmatory assays only in the context of compatible symptoms or ileus/toxic megacolon.
